entities.summary:
Herodorus of Megara, a colossal figure literally and figuratively, dominated the ancient Greek musical world as a trumpet player (salpinktes) during the 4th century BCE. His unparalleled success at the Olympic Games, where he secured ten consecutive victories in the trumpet contest, cemented his legend as a performer whose prowess transcended mere musicianship to become a spectacle of physical might and sonic power. While precise birth and death dates remain elusive, his career peaked around the mid-4th century BCE, placing him firmly within the Classical Era, a period when athletic and artistic excellence were deeply intertwined with civic pride and religious devotion across the Hellenic world. His fame extended beyond the Peloponnese, influencing perceptions of musical performance and athletic achievement from Megara to Olympia.

Herodorus's legendary career was defined by his extraordinary physical attributes and the sheer volume of his playing. Ancient sources, notably Athenaeus in his Deipnosophistae, recount his immense size and lung capacity, claiming he could blow two trumpets simultaneously and that his sound could carry for miles. His ten Olympic victories, achieved between approximately 368 BCE and 332 BCE, made him an unprecedented champion in a contest that tested not only musical skill but also endurance and projection. Beyond the Olympics, he was said to have accompanied military campaigns, using his powerful salpinx to rally troops and intimidate enemies, embodying the dual martial and ceremonial roles of the ancient trumpet.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Herodorus's unparalleled ten Olympic victories in the trumpet contest established a unique record for sustained excellence in ancient Greek competitive performance, influencing cultural perceptions of spectacle and individual achievement. His legendary physical capabilities contributed to the historical record of extreme human performance, resonating through later accounts like Athenaeus's.
